paras: The Rockmart tunnel riot was a gunfight on July 15, 1882, at a railroad tunnel in Paulding County, Georgia, about seven miles from Rockmart, after a white man, John Hicks, tried without authority to disarm Black railroad hands. Hicks's party shot a Black worker named Tom Laws, who was reported dying and later dead, and the Black workers then killed Hicks. The papers treated it as a race riot, and it ended in the arrest of some thirty Black workers, four life sentences for murder and a death sentence for a man called the riot's leader.

The tunnel was being cut on the Rome extension of the Cincinnati and Georgia railroad, which a Georgia paper called the Macon and Brunswick extension, and its Black laborers worked for a contractor named McKechney. According to a National Associated Press dispatch, two men forced out of Polk County by its local-option liquor law had opened a saloon at the tunnel mouth, frequented by white men it called 'desperate characters.' The Marietta Journal said George Foote kept the bar room, where the workers 'fiddled, danced and drank whiskey,' and that John Hicks, 'a quarrelsome rowdy,' had caused several disturbances there.

On the Thursday before, white farmers selling peaches and watermelons at the camp accused a Black boy of stealing fruit, and one of them aimed a gun at him. As the sellers left, one fired a shotgun at the workers, and some fifty shots were exchanged in a running fight that left the farmers' wagon wrecked but, by one account, no one hurt. The same dispatch said Hicks had earlier shot a timber worker named Hagan, and that many of the hands had since armed themselves 'for self-protection.'

On Saturday, payday, Hicks came to the bar room with his young son and George Foote Jr. and began taking the workers' pistols, falsely claiming to be an officer. Several men gave up their weapons, but one refused; the Atlanta wire named him as Tom Laws and said he 'was shot by the Hicks party,' while a Rockmart letter to the Rome Courier said Hicks shot him four times and Foote once, by Foote's own account. The workers then fired on Hicks, who ran and was killed near where the fight began, struck by eight to ten bullets.

Several Black men were wounded, put at four in some reports and six in another, and Foote escaped with slight wounds. Hicks's son was captured by the workers and released because of his age, and the workers broke into Foote's house looking for him and took over the bar room.

On Sunday the sheriffs of Paulding and Polk counties came with posses armed with shotguns; the workers at first refused to surrender but then gave up, and twenty-five to thirty-three were jailed at Dallas. The prisoners waived a committal hearing, and the Paulding grand jury returned true bills against seven men for murder and twenty-seven for riot. In early August, Paulding Superior Court sentenced Jerry Ganaway, Henry Lacy, Rufus Williams and William Daniell to life for murder, gave a man named Brown two years for assault with intent to murder, sentenced seventeen to twelve months for riot and discharged six.

Wm. Slaughter, described as the leader of the riot, escaped, was arrested in Campbell County, Tennessee, in September and brought back by Sheriff W. C. Matthews. In December he was convicted of Hicks's murder and sentenced to hang on February 2, 1883, and a motion for a new trial was filed. No report of an inquest into Tom Laws's death, or of any charge against Hicks's companions, appears in the coverage.

An Atlanta dispatch of July 17 carried the story nationally under headlines such as 'A Riot Between the Races' and 'Riot Between Negroes and Whites,' and it was still running in a Rhode Island weekly as 'Whisky Riot' at month's end. That wire blamed 'reckless white men' and whisky and said Hicks acted without authority, while a shorter version reduced the event to Hicks being killed 'by a gang of negro laborers.' A widely copied 'Particulars' paragraph called Hicks 'a desperado' yet described the workers 'forming a mob' and attacking him 'with great ferocity.'

Georgia papers gave the fullest accounts: the Marietta Journal called Hicks a rowdy who posed as an officer but stressed that some workers shot him 'several times after he was dead,' and the Rome Courier's correspondent blamed 'lawless whisky sellers.' Foote used the Atlanta Constitution to deny that he had sold whisky at the tunnel. Once the trials ended, the Savannah Morning News called the riot a 'disgraceful affair' and the convictions 'an instance of speedy justice following crime,' and the Knoxville Daily Chronicle headed its report on Slaughter 'A Murderer Arrested.'

Accounts differ on the Black casualties: most say one man was killed or mortally wounded, but the Marietta Journal's Dallas correspondent wrote that 'none' were killed, and the Knoxville account three months later called the man, named there as 'Gabe,' only badly wounded. The Knoxville report, built on the sheriff's account, also said the contractor had armed his workers and that some 300 of them joined the shooting, and it described Hicks as a man 'employed as a boss' rather than the rowdy of the Georgia reports.

reader.title: Rockmart tunnel riot
bases: A white man, John Hicks, backed by several other white men and without legal authority, tried to disarm Black railroad hands and shot one who refused, setting off a gunfight in which Hicks was killed and Black workers were wounded (A3, A14, A15).

The Atlanta wire, two independent Marietta Journal items, a Rockmart letter to the Rome Courier and a separate National Associated Press dispatch agree that Hicks's attempt to disarm the Black workers led to a fight in which he was killed (A3, A13, A14, A15, A16).

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Reckless white men and Black railroad hands clashed at a whisky bar at the tunnel; Hicks, acting without authority, tried to disarm the Black men, his party shot Tom Laws, and the Black men then killed Hicks.

accounts.label: Short Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: A 'drunken row' started, the white men tried to disarm the Black laborers, one Black man was mortally wounded and 'a gang of negro laborers' killed Hicks.

accounts.label: Marietta Journal (local)
accounts.gist: Hicks, posing as an officer, entered Foote's bar room with his son and disarmed several dancers; one refused and exchanged shots and fell mortally wounded, after which Hicks was riddled with bullets.

accounts.label: Dallas correspondent
accounts.gist: Foote and Hicks, for unknown reasons, angered the Black workers and both sides opened fire; Hicks was killed and several Black men wounded but 'none killed'.

accounts.label: Rockmart letter (Whitehead)
accounts.gist: Hicks and Foote took several pistols; the man who refused was shot four times by Hicks and once by Foote, 'so he says', and the crowd then charged and killed Hicks.

accounts.label: National Associated Press dispatch
accounts.gist: Saloon men driven from Polk County and the 'desperado' Hicks had provoked the camp for weeks; the workers had armed for self-protection, and Hicks's disarming on payday led to a fight leaving Hicks and one Black man dead and six wounded.

accounts.label: Knoxville Daily Chronicle (after Slaughter's arrest)
accounts.gist: The contractor had armed his hands; Hicks, 'employed as a boss', tried to disarm them, 'Gabe' was badly wounded, and some 300 armed Black men killed Hicks while his boys pleaded for his life.
